{{short description|Sea level and coastal erosion calculation}}
[[File:Norfolk Beach, Coochiemudlo Island, coast erosion 02.jpg|thumb|Shoreline recession of a sandy shore at Norfolk Beach, Coochiemuldo Island, Australia]]
The '''Bruun rule''' is a [[formula]] for estimating the magnitude of the retreat of the [[shore]]line of a sandy shore in response to [[Sea level#Change|changes in sea level]].  Originally published in 1962 by [[Per Moller Bruun]],<ref name="Bruun 1962">{{Cite journal|last=Bruun|first=Per Moler|date=1962|title=Sea-Level Rise as a Cause of Shore Erosion|journal=American Society of Civil Engineers Journal of the Waterways and Harbours Division|volume=88|pages=117–130}}</ref> the Bruun rule was the first to give a relationship between [[sea level rise]] and [[Coastal erosion|shoreline recession]].<ref name="Grilli 2017">{{Cite journal|last1=Grilli|first1=Annette|last2=Spaulding|first2=Malcolm L.|last3=Oakley|first3=Bryan A.|last4=Damon|first4=Chris|date=2017-04-19|title=Mapping the coastal risk for the next century, including sea level rise and changes in the coastline: application to Charlestown RI, USA|journal=Natural Hazards|language=en|volume=88|issue=1|pages=389–414|doi=10.1007/s11069-017-2871-x|bibcode=2017NatHa..88..389G |s2cid=54176474 |issn=0921-030X}}</ref> The rule is a simple, [[Two-dimensional space|two dimensional]] [[mass]] conversion, and remains in common use to estimate shoreline recession in response to sea level rise, despite criticism and modification, and the availability of more complex alternate models.<ref name="Ranasinghe 2009">{{Cite journal |last1=Ranasinghe |first1=Roshanka |last2=Stive |first2=Marcel J. F. |date=2009-05-16 |title=Rising seas and retreating coastlines |url=https://repository.tudelft.nl/islandora/object/uuid%3A2a14576d-03de-4775-9ecc-9e4be0dbe7c8/datastream/OBJ/download |journal=[[Climatic Change]] |language=en |volume=97 |issue=3–4 |pages=465–468 |doi=10.1007/s10584-009-9593-3 |bibcode=2009ClCh...97..465R |issn=0165-0009 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

==The calculation==
The Bruun rule gives a [[Correlation and dependence|linear relationship]] between [[sea level rise]] and [[coastal erosion|shoreline recession]] based on equilibrium profile theory, which asserts that [[shore]] face profile maintains an equilibrium shape, and as sea level rises the increasing [[Accommodation (geology)|accommodation space]] forces this equilibrium profile landward and upward to preserve its shape relative to the new sea level.<ref name="Aagaard 2012">{{Cite journal|last1=Aagaard|first1=Troels|last2=Sørensen|first2=Per|date=2012-01-02|title=Coastal profile response to sea level rise: a process-based approach|journal=Earth Surface Processes and Landforms|language=en|volume=37|issue=3|pages=354–362|doi=10.1002/esp.2271|bibcode=2012ESPL...37..354A |s2cid=128939907 |issn=0197-9337}}</ref> As such, the Bruun rule analysis assumes that the upper [[beach]] is eroded as the shore profile moves landward, and that the volume of [[erosion|eroded]] material is deposited offshore, resulting in a rise of the nearshore [[seabed|bottom]] which maintains a constant water depth.<ref name="SCOR 1991">{{Cite journal|author=Scientific Committee on Ocean Research (SCOR) Working Group 89|date=Summer 1991|title=The Response of Beaches to Sea-Level Changes: A Review of Predictive Models|journal=Journal of Coastal Research|volume=7|pages=895–921|jstor=}}</ref> The Bruun rule predicts [[Coastal erosion|coastal recession]] to be as much as 10 to 50 times [[sea level rise]], depending on the [[slope]] of the [[beach]].<ref name="Le Cozannet 2014">{{Cite journal|last1=Le Cozannet|first1=Gonéri|last2=Garcin|first2=Manuel|last3=Yates|first3=Marissa|last4=Idier|first4=Déborah|last5=Meyssignac|first5=Benoit|date=November 2014|title=Approaches to evaluate the recent impacts of sea-level rise on shoreline changes|journal=Earth-Science Reviews|volume=138|pages=47–60|doi=10.1016/j.earscirev.2014.08.005|bibcode=2014ESRv..138...47L |issn=0012-8252|doi-access=free}}</ref>

[[File:The Bruun Rule SCOR 1991.JPG|thumb|Illustration of the Bruun rule, by the Scientific Committee on Ocean Research (1991)]]

The mathematical notation of the Bruun rule is:

<math>R = \frac{SL}{h+B} = \frac{S}{\tan\beta}</math><ref name="Anderson 2015">{{Cite journal|last1=Anderson|first1=Tiffany R.|last2=Fletcher|first2=Charles H.|last3=Barbee|first3=Matthew M.|last4=Frazer|first4=L. Neil|last5=Romine|first5=Bradley M.|date=2015-03-18|title=Doubling of coastal erosion under rising sea level by mid-century in Hawaii|journal=Natural Hazards|language=en|volume=78|issue=1|pages=75–103|doi=10.1007/s11069-015-1698-6|bibcode=2015NatHa..78...75A |s2cid=51683359 |issn=0921-030X}}</ref><ref name="Ranasinghe 2009" />

Where,

*''R'' is [[Coastal erosion|shoreline recession]], in metres
*''S'' is [[sea level rise]], in metres
*''L'' is the horizontal length of the bottom affected by the [[sea level rise]] (from the [[dune]] peak to depth of closure), in metres
*''h'' is the depth of closure (the water depth beyond which significant [[sediment transport]] does not occur<ref name="Baron 2014">{{Cite journal|last1=Baron|first1=Heather M.|last2=Ruggiero|first2=Peter|last3=Wood|first3=Nathan J.|last4=Harris|first4=Erica L.|last5=Allan|first5=Jonathan|last6=Komar|first6=Paul D.|last7=Corcoran|first7=Patrick|date=2014-09-13|title=Incorporating climate change and morphological uncertainty into coastal change hazard assessments|journal=Natural Hazards|language=en|volume=75|issue=3|pages=2081–2102|doi=10.1007/s11069-014-1417-8|issn=0921-030X|doi-access=free|hdl=10.1007/s11069-014-1417-8|hdl-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Rollason 2010">{{Cite book|url=http://www.coastalconference.com/2010/papers2010/Verity%20Rollason%20full%20paper.pdf|title=Assessing Shoreline Response to Sea Level Rise: An Alternative to the Bruun Rule|last1=Rollason|first1=R.|last2=Patterson|first2=D.|last3=Huxley|first3=C.|publisher=NSW Coastal Conference|year=2010}}</ref>), in metres
*''B'' is the dune height above sea level, in metres
*''β'' is the average [[slope]] of the active profile<ref name="Anderson 2015" />

== History ==
In 1954, Per Moller Bruun published a paper<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Bruun|first=Per|date=1954|title=Coast erosion and the development of beach profiles.|journal=Technical Memorandum|volume=44|page=82}}</ref> describing beach profiles and cross shore equilibrium.<ref name="Cooper 2004" /> Developing on these ideas, in 1962 he published his paper "Sea-Level Rise as a Cause of Shore Erosion",''<ref name="Bruun 1962" />'' which first gave a relationship between [[sea level rise]] and the [[Coastal erosion|shoreline recession]] of equilibrium beach profiles.<ref name="Grilli 2017" /> His rule wasn't given a name until 1967, when Schwartz published "The Bruun Theory of Sea-Level Rise as a Cause of Shore Erosion" which detailed [[laboratory]] and [[field experiment|field]] tests of the theory and concluded that "the concept henceforth be known as 'Bruun's Rule'."<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Schwartz|first=Maurice|date=1967|title=The Bruun Theory of Sea-Level Rise as a Cause of Shore Erosion|jstor=30084988|journal=The Journal of Geology|volume=75|issue=1|pages=76–92|doi=10.1086/627232|bibcode=1967JG.....75...76S |s2cid=129215193 }}</ref>

Per Bruun has since published works to clarify the limitations and practicality of his model, including "Review of Conditions for Uses of the Bruun Rule of Erosion" in 1983,<ref name="Bruun 1983" /> and "The Bruun Rule of Erosion by Sea-Level Rise: A Discussion on Large-Scale Two- and Three- Dimensional Usages" in 1988.<ref name="Bruun 1988" /> These publications outline the rule's limitations and practicality and stress that, though this model is intentionally [[Two-dimensional space|two dimensional]], it is applied to [[Three-dimensional space|three dimensional]] environments in practice.<ref name="Bruun 1983" /><ref name="Bruun 1988" /> Bruun states that the rule "must be subjected to realistic adjustments"<ref name="Bruun 1983" /> for practical use.

As Bruun acknowledges, the Bruun rule is a characteristically simple rule and has therefore been modified many times over, to account for more factors and in order to be accurately applicable in more cases.<ref name="Rosati 2013">{{Cite journal|last1=Rosati|first1=J.|last2=Dean|first2=R.|last3=Walton|first3=T.|date=2013|title=The modified Bruun Rule extended for landward transport|journal=Marine Geology|volume=340|pages=71–81|doi=10.1016/j.margeo.2013.04.018|bibcode=2013MGeol.340...71R |s2cid=13792861 |url=https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1218&context=usarmyresearch}}</ref> bThe Bruun rule has been most often modified to account for [[Longshore drift|longshore transport]], [[overwash]], and [[Aeolian processes|Aeolian sediment transport]].''<ref name="Rosati 2013" />'' For example, Dean and Maurmeier in 1983 modified the rule to be applicable to barrier shores and islands, some of which experience accretion instead of erosion.<ref name="Aagaard 2012" /><ref name="Zhang 2004" /> Rosati et al. in 2013<ref name="Rosati 2013" /> and Dean and Houston in 2016<ref name="Dean 2016">{{Cite journal|last1=Dean|first1=R.G.|last2=Houston|first2=J.R.|date=August 2016|title=Determining shoreline response to sea level rise|journal=Coastal Engineering|volume=114|pages=1–8|doi=10.1016/j.coastaleng.2016.03.009|bibcode=2016CoasE.114....1D |issn=0378-3839}}</ref> have modified the rule to account for onshore transport, and cross shore movement over the supposed depth of closure.<ref name="Rosati 2013" /><ref name="Dean 2016" /> Further, Ashton et al. in 2011 modified the Bruun rule for use on [[cliffed coast]]s,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ashton|first1=Andrew D.|last2=Walkden|first2=Mike J.A.|last3=Dickson|first3=Mark E.|date=June 2011|title=Equilibrium responses of cliffed coasts to changes in the rate of sea level rise|journal=Marine Geology|volume=284|issue=1–4|pages=217–229|doi=10.1016/j.margeo.2011.01.007|bibcode=2011MGeol.284..217A |issn=0025-3227}}</ref> and Hinkel et al. in 2013 used the rule as part of a wider methodology to describe the effects on [[sea level rise]] on and around [[Inlet|tidal inlets]].<ref name="Hinkel 2013">{{Cite journal|last1=Hinkel|first1=Jochen|last2=Nicholls|first2=Robert J.|last3=Tol|first3=Richard S.J.|last4=Wang|first4=Zheng B.|last5=Hamilton|first5=Jacqueline M.|last6=Boot|first6=Gerben|last7=Vafeidis|first7=Athanasios T.|last8=McFadden|first8=Loraine|last9=Ganopolski|first9=Andrey|date=December 2013|title=A global analysis of erosion of sandy beaches and sea-level rise: An application of DIVA|journal=Global and Planetary Change|volume=111|pages=150–158|doi=10.1016/j.gloplacha.2013.09.002|bibcode=2013GPC...111..150H|issn=0921-8181}}</ref> The biggest challenge that remains seems to be isolating the effect of [[sea level rise]] on beach morphology from the coupled effects of wave energy, tidal currents, wind action, sediment supplies, sediment types and grain size, among others.<ref name="Davidson-Arnott 2005">{{Cite journal|last=Davidson-Arnott|first=Robin G. D.|date=November 2005|title=Conceptual Model of the Effects of Sea Level Rise on Sandy Coasts|journal=Journal of Coastal Research|language=en-US|volume=216|pages=1166–1172|doi=10.2112/03-0051.1|s2cid=129063968 |issn=0749-0208|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Cooper 2004" />

In various forms and coupled with other models, the Bruun rule has now been used to estimate shoreline responses to [[sea level rise]] worldwide.<ref name="Le Cozannet 2014" /> The Bruun rule has been applied to [[coast]]s including of the [[Caspian Sea]],<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Neshaei|first1=M. A. == Criticisms ==
The effect of [[climate change]] on beaches is challenging to accurately model, as it is an interdisciplinary subject that involves [[ocean science|ocean]], [[earth science|earth]], and [[atmospheric sciences|atmospheric]] science as well as [[civil engineering]] and [[policy analysis|policy]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Vitousek|first1=Sean|last2=Barnard|first2=Patrick L.|last3=Limber|first3=Patrick|date=2017|title=Can beaches survive climate change?|journal=Journal of Geophysical Research: Earth Surface|language=en|volume=122|issue=4|pages=1060–1067|doi=10.1002/2017jf004308|bibcode=2017JGRF..122.1060V |issn=2169-9003|doi-access=free}}</ref> Reliable coastal climate change impact assessments are needed to underpin effective strategies of adaptation in order to prepare growing coastal communities and high value coastal assets.<ref name="Ranasinghe 2016">{{Cite journal|last=Ranasinghe|first=Roshanka|date=2016|title=Assessing climate change impacts on open sandy coasts: A review|journal=Earth-Science Reviews|volume=160|pages=320–332|doi=10.1016/j.earscirev.2016.07.011|bibcode=2016ESRv..160..320R |issn=0012-8252|doi-access=free}}</ref>  As a result, models for estimating coastal erosion as a result of sea level rise - including the Bruun rule and models based on the Bruun rule - are constantly being reviewed and updated.<ref name="Anderson 2015" /><ref name="Baron 2014" /><ref name="Rollason 2010" /> The Bruun rule has become the centre of much academic debate.<ref name="Hinkel 2013" />

In response to its inherent assumptions, the Bruun rule has been widely criticised.<ref name="Aagaard 2012" /><ref name="Anderson 2015" />''<ref name="Rollason 2010" /><ref name="Ranasinghe 2016" /><ref name="Ranasinghe 2012">{{Cite journal|last1=Ranasinghe|first1=Roshanka|last2=Callaghan|first2=David|last3=Stive|first3=Marcel|date=2012|title=Estimating coastal recession due to sea level rise: beyond the Bruun rule|journal=Climatic Change|volume=110|issue=3–4|pages=561–574|doi=10.1007/s10584-011-0107-8|bibcode=2012ClCh..110..561R |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Atkinson 2018">{{Cite journal|last1=Atkinson|first1=Alexander|last2=Baldock|first2=Tom|last3=Birrien|first3=Florent|last4=David|first4=Callaghan|last5=Nielsen|first5=Peter|last6=Beuzen|first6=Tomas|last7=Turner|first7=Ian|last8=Blenkinsopp|first8=Chris|last9=Ranasinghe|first9=Roshanka|date=2018|title=Laboratory investigation of the Bruun Rule and beach response to sea level rise|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378383917302648|journal=Coastal Engineering|volume=136|issue=4|pages=183–202|doi=10.1016/s0378-3839(98)00043-x|issn=0378-3839|via=Elsevier Science Direct|url-access=subscription}}</ref>''<ref name="Cooper 2004">{{Cite journal|last1=Cooper|first1=J. Andrew G.|last2=Pilkey|first2=Orrin H.|date=November 2004|title=Sea-level rise and shoreline retreat: time to abandon the Bruun Rule|journal=Global and Planetary Change|volume=43|issue=3–4|pages=157–171|doi=10.1016/j.gloplacha.2004.07.001|bibcode=2004GPC....43..157C |issn=0921-8181}}</ref> Some of the rule's most criticised assumptions include the nonexistence of [[gradient]]s in [[Longshore drift|longshore sediment transport]], the existence of a depth of closure, a closed [[Sedimentary budget|sediment budget]], and the availability of sufficient [[sand]] sources.<ref name="Aagaard 2012" /> In 2015, Andersen et al. labelled the Bruun rule as " on its own...virtually unusable in open-ocean coastal environments"<ref name="Anderson 2015" /> due to its assumptions of [[Biophysical environment|physical environmental]] setting.<ref name="Anderson 2015" />

One prominently criticised assumption of the Bruun rule is its postulation of the net effects of longshore transport as negligible,<ref name="Aagaard 2012" /><ref name="Anderson 2015" /><ref name="Cooper 2004" /> as the rule is by definition a two dimensional cross shore model that does not account for the longshore third dimension.<ref name="Ranasinghe 2009" /> These longshore effects can, however, be the major cause of [[sediment]] erosion or [[Deposition (geology)|deposition]] along beaches, dominating shoreline morphology and even masking the impacts of sea level rise as described by the Bruun Model.<ref name="Aagaard 2012" /><ref name="Anderson 2015" />

Another criticised assumption is the existence of a 'depth of closure'. The depth of closure is considered to be the water depth beyond which there are no significant changes in bed level, and is usually taken as the boundary between the [[upper shoreface]], characterised by breaking [[Wind wave|waves]] and [[Shoal|bars]], and the [[lower shoreface]], characterised by nonbreaking waves and a lack of bars.<ref name="Aagaard 2012" /> The Bruun rule stipulates that there is no significant [[sediment]] transfer across this boundary, however the strength of this concept in practice is debated.<ref name="Aagaard 2012" /><ref name="Cooper 2004" /> The alternative R-DA model, proposed by Davidson-Arnott,<ref name="Davidson-Arnott 2005" /> is based on the same assumptions as the Bruun rule, except it recognises significant sediment transfer between the upper and lower shoreface, hypothesising that sediment is eroded from the lower shoreface and transported to the upper shoreface to maintain an equilibrium profile, and that as a result there is an upward and landward migration of the depth of closure with sea level rise.<ref name="Aagaard 2012" /><ref name="Davidson-Arnott 2005" />

Cooper and Pilkey have been direct in their criticism of the Bruun rule, publishing a paper in 2004 titled "Sea-level rise and shoreline retreat: time to abandon the Bruun Rule",<ref name="Cooper 2004" /> which is regularly cited in ensuing literature.'''<ref name="Cooper 2004" />''' They argue that despite widespread criticism, the original Bruun rule continues to be applied in inappropriate contexts, as outlined by Bruun<ref name="Bruun 1988" /> and experimental history, and that the Bruun rule and its accompanying controversial assumptions are embedded in later models claiming to offer more sophisticated insights into coastal behaviour.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=French|first1=Jon|last2=Payo|first2=Andres|last3=Murray|first3=Brad|last4=Orford|first4=Julian|last5=Eliot|first5=Matt|last6=Cowell|first6=Peter|date=March 2016|title=Appropriate complexity for the prediction of coastal and estuarine geomorphic behaviour at decadal to centennial scales|journal=Geomorphology|volume=256|pages=3–16|doi=10.1016/j.geomorph.2015.10.005|bibcode=2016Geomo.256....3F |issn=0169-555X|doi-access=free}}</ref> Cooper and Pilkey describe the use of the Bruun rule as "a "one model fits all" approach"<ref name="Cooper 2004" /> to a range of complex coastal environments for which it is unfit to describe.<ref name="Cooper 2004" /> They list three main reasons that the rule "does not work":<ref name="Cooper 2004" /> its restrictive assumptions, the omission of important [[Variable and attribute (research)|variables]], and its reliance on outdated and erroneous concepts.<ref name="Cooper 2004" /> They describe the rule's restrictive assumptions as a closed materials balance, which ignores net [[Longshore drift|longshore transport]], and the lack of an accretionary component, that assumes [[sea level rise]] always results in [[Coastal erosion|beach recession]], which together limit the rule's use to a small number of coasts.<ref name="Cooper 2004" /> Cooper and Pilkey list the omitted [[Variable and attribute (research)|variables]] as the presence of [[outcrop]]s or bottom [[Ocean current|currents]], the effect of [[continental shelf]] [[slope]] on retreat rate, site specific feedback relationships, and the highly variable patterns of coastal evolution at millennial [[Geologic time scale|time scales]], and the outdated and erroneous concepts relied upon as a universal equilibrium profile theory, a closure depth, and that unsupported idea that shoreface steepness has an effect on the rate of shore retreat.<ref name="Cooper 2004" /> They "conclude that [the Bruun rule] has outlived its usefulness and should be abandoned",<ref name="Cooper 2004" /> however they have been criticised for providing no "meaningful alternative"<ref name="Rosati 2013" /> to the rule.

In his papers,<ref name="Bruun 1962" /><ref name="Bruun 1983">{{Cite journal|last=Bruun|first=Per|date=February 1983|title=Review of conditions for uses of the Bruun rule of erosion|journal=Coastal Engineering|volume=7|issue=1|pages=77–89|doi=10.1016/0378-3839(83)90028-5|bibcode=1983CoasE...7...77B |issn=0378-3839}}</ref><ref name="Bruun 1988">{{Cite journal|last=Bruun|first=Per|date=1988-10-07|title=The Bruun Rule of Erosion by Sea-Level Rise: A Discussion on Large-Scale Two- and Three-Dimensional Usages|url=http://journals.fcla.edu/jcr/article/view/77813|journal=Journal of Coastal Research|language=en|volume=4|issue=4|issn=0749-0208|access-date=2018-11-09|archive-date=2019-05-31|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190531182946/http://journals.fcla.edu/jcr/article/view/77813|url-status=dead}}</ref> Bruun did not present a rigorous mathematical derivation for his rule, which has caused confusion in the [[Scientific community|research community]].<ref name="Zhang 2004">{{Cite journal|last1=Zhang|first1=Keqi|last2=Douglas|first2=Bruce C.|last3=Leatherman|first3=Stephen P.|date=May 2004|title=Global Warming and Coastal Erosion|journal=Climatic Change|language=en|volume=64|issue=1/2|pages=41–58|doi=10.1023/b:clim.0000024690.32682.48|bibcode=2004ClCh...64...41Z |s2cid=154185819 |issn=0165-0009}}</ref> For example, Rosen in 1978, Allison and Schwartz in 1981, Dean and Maurmeyer in 1983, and Zhang, Douglas and Leatherman in 2004 have all mathematically derived the Bruun rule differently, with disagreement on the assumptions and limitations of the Bruun rule unique to their own derivations.<ref name="Zhang 2004" /> However, the latter revision by Zhang et al.<ref name="Zhang 2004" /> presents an alternative derivation showing that "even though very simple, the Bruun model has considerable generality".<ref name="Zhang 2004" />

Some field and laboratory tests have supported the Bruun rule, although claimed [[experiment]]al flaws in these publications have been criticised.<ref name="Anderson 2015" /> Amongst others, Ranasinghe and Stive in 2009,<ref name="Ranasinghe 2009" /> and later Andersen et al. in 2015,<ref name="Anderson 2015" /> have concluded that "no study has produced comprehensive, well-accepted verification of the Brunn model".<ref name="Anderson 2015" /> However, there is a near consensus that the basic [[Qualitative research|qualitative]] model of shoreline recession is valid,<ref name="Ranasinghe 2009" /><ref name="Anderson 2015" /><ref name="SCOR 1991" /> despite [[Quantitative research|quantitative]] data gleaned from the Bruun rule being dubbed as "very coarse approximations"<ref name="Anderson 2015" /> or "broadly indicative estimates".<ref name="Ranasinghe 2009" /> Despite these criticisms, the Bruun rule is credited for its simplicity, and there remains "no simple, viable alternative".<ref name="Rosati 2013" />
